proposals.relationship: Quinn recalls Weber naming Febvre among the formative historians he read when developing his own historical practice.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated by Frederick Quinn’s account of a 1966 reading course: he asked Weber which works and authors had formed him. Plural credit includes Febvre, Bloch, Braudel and Robert Mandrou. Quinn’s discussion connects those readings with interdisciplinary social and cultural inquiry; it does not establish adoption of every Annales method or a particular monograph. The checked HTML’s note 4 is malformed, so most exact titles/editions are not recoverable; originals unread.
primary_locators: Quinn 2009, unpaginated HTML recollection beginning I had only one reading course, then Weber smiled, then He ticked off titles; succeeding history-from-below/mentalités discussion and note 4.

proposals.relationship: Weber invokes Elias’s account of restraint to frame his own reflections on the policing and recurrence of social violence.
proposals.evidence_note: Own letter to Frederick Quinn dated 4 August 1981, published by Quinn in 2009. This is a specific conceptual use within a speculative private reflection, not proof of his whole fascism interpretation or endorsement of his empirical/political generalizations. Quinn’s note 33 cites a 2000 revised edition of The Civilizing Process; that later editorial reference is not the edition Weber read in 1981. Original manuscript and Elias book unread.
primary_locators: Quinn 2009, letter headed August 4, 1981, paragraph beginning I have been reading about fascism again, through the Elias reference and following reflection; editorial n. 33.

proposals.relationship: Weber uses the Tillys’ distinction between local protest and national political action to test claims about peasant politicization in 1848–1851.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1980 article p. 524/n. 10 sets his definition beside the more stringent formulation in Charles, Louise and Richard Tilly’s The Rebellious Century (1975), p. 289; p. 528/n. 32 explicitly uses their pre-political-action concept. All three retain credit. No agreement with their entire theory or direct reading of the complete 1975 book is asserted. A separate Tilly criticism of Weber coexists.
primary_locators: French Historical Studies11:4 (Autumn1980), printed p. 524, definition of politics and n. 10; printed p. 528, paragraph beginning John Merriman has written and n. 32.

proposals.relationship: Tilly challenges Weber’s image of an isolated traditional countryside transformed after 1870, emphasizing earlier markets, class divisions and national politics.
proposals.evidence_note: Tilly’s December 1978 draft opening was read in the university PDF text extraction; subsequent download/screenshots returned errors or the repository app shell. Michael Burns’s 1984 p. 5 independently and substantively attributes this criticism and Tilly’s alternative emphasis on capitalism/state-making. Burns’s original is successfully available locally; precise later published Tilly chapter wording is not presumed identical to the draft. Tilly praises Weber’s ethnographic richness while disputing the model; Weber’s complete 1976 book and Tilly’s later chapter remain unread.
primary_locators: Tilly CRSO189 December1978, one-based PDF pp. 2–5: opening Peasants into Frenchmen, evidence critique beginning Weber draws his evidence, timing/market/class analysis and Familiarity is not truth; Burns1984 printed p. 5, paragraph beginning And provocative it was and note-call11.

proposals.relationship: Judt uses Weber’s account of interwar decline and insecurity to establish the prewar background of Vichy and postwar France.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1996 review essay explicitly draws on The Hollow Years for demographic/political mood and the desire for peace, then contrasts Michael B. Miller’s more optimistic account. Judt’s criticism of Miller is not assigned to Weber. This is identifiable argumentative use, not formative influence or agreement with every Weber interpretation. Full Weber book unread.
primary_locators: France Without Glory, NYRB23 May1996, section1: paragraphs beginning Any account of the condition, The demographic evidence, There is no doubt and Eugen Weber brings out very well; following Miller contrast.
